question.prompt: What effect comes from saying the clock was trying to make commuters punctual?

options.text: It humorously gives the clock a human intention
it proves the clock has a hidden alarm
it accuses the technician of dishonesty
it explains how the mechanism works

question.explanation: A clock cannot intend to influence behaviour, so the phrase personifies it. The joke links its fast time with commuters' punctuality without explaining a mechanism.

stimulus.title: A clock that gained a story
stimulus.body:
For years the station clock had been five minutes fast. Commuters joked that it was trying to make them punctual. Then a technician reset it. The next morning, people gathered under its newly accurate hands and compared watches.

'It used to be reliable,' one traveller complained.

'It is reliable now,' the technician said.

Both were using the word differently. The traveller had known exactly how far wrong the clock was and had adjusted mentally. The repair removed that familiar error. For a few days, old habits made accurate time feel surprising.

The station manager put up a notice: 'Clock corrected on Monday. Please check your usual adjustment.' By Friday, the jokes had changed. People said the clock had finally decided to catch the train itself. The technician kept the old maintenance note, not as an instruction for the next repair, but as a reminder that changing a machine can also require changing the habits around it.

workedSolution: A clock cannot intend to influence behaviour, so the phrase personifies it.
The joke links its fast time with commuters' punctuality without explaining a mechanism.
reviewFocus: Independently solve without the key; check each alternative and the stated conditions.
Review originality, vocabulary, difficulty and time for an above-average Year 5/6 learner.

question.prompt: What happens to both models before the tub is rocked?
question.explanation: The passage says both float on still water. Their different performance appears under disturbance, so still-water success alone does not compare stability.

stimulus.title: The floating garden model
stimulus.body:
In this fictional design challenge, pupils built model gardens that could float in a tub. Team Pine used a wide shallow tray and arranged equal masses of clay evenly around its edge. Team Reed used a narrow tray and piled its clay in the centre. Both models floated on still water.

When a volunteer rocked the tub, Pine's tray remained level longer. Reed's tray tipped and took in water. Reed's team wanted to replace all its clay with lighter material. Pine's team suggested first moving some of the existing clay lower and spreading it more evenly.

The teams agreed to change only the clay arrangement on Reed's tray for the next test. They kept the total clay mass and the tray unchanged. The second test would investigate distribution, not establish the best possible garden design. To compare tray widths fairly later, they would need another test with equal loads and similar arrangements. No model would be placed in a real creek; the challenge was a classroom investigation of design choices.

question.prompt: What action does the lunch article recommend trying first?
question.explanation: The recommendation explicitly prioritises trying two serving points. Extra lunch minutes remain an option if the first trial fails, so they are not the initial change.

stimulus.title: The case for a slower lunch
stimulus.body:
Our student council proposes adding five minutes to lunch, taking those minutes from the transition period before afternoon lessons. A recent student survey found that many pupils felt hurried while eating. However, a feeling of hurry does not by itself tell us how the timetable should change.

For two weeks, volunteers recorded when the queue opened, when the last meal was served and when tables were cleared. On busy days, the last pupils had only eight minutes before the bell. On quiet days, most pupils finished comfortably. The queue seemed to be the main difficulty, not the length of lunch for everyone.

We therefore recommend trying two serving points before changing lesson transitions. This requires a staffing check, and it may not solve the problem. If the late-served pupils still have too little time, the extra minutes should be reconsidered. The survey raised the question; observation helped us choose the first change to test. Neither should be ignored, but they do different jobs.

workedSolution: The recommendation explicitly prioritises trying two serving points.
Extra lunch minutes remain an option if the first trial fails, so they are not the initial change.
reviewFocus: Independently solve without the key; check each alternative and the stated conditions.
Review originality, vocabulary, difficulty and time for an above-average Year 5/6 learner.

question.prompt: Why does the article distinguish the survey from observation?

options.text: One identifies concern and the other helps locate a possible cause
the survey must be false because feelings are involved
observation guarantees the proposed solution works
the two sources cover unrelated topics

question.explanation: The survey shows pupils feel hurried, while queue timing indicates where the pressure arises. Both contribute evidence of different kinds without proving the serving-point solution in advance.

stimulus.title: The case for a slower lunch
stimulus.body:
Our student council proposes adding five minutes to lunch, taking those minutes from the transition period before afternoon lessons. A recent student survey found that many pupils felt hurried while eating. However, a feeling of hurry does not by itself tell us how the timetable should change.

For two weeks, volunteers recorded when the queue opened, when the last meal was served and when tables were cleared. On busy days, the last pupils had only eight minutes before the bell. On quiet days, most pupils finished comfortably. The queue seemed to be the main difficulty, not the length of lunch for everyone.

We therefore recommend trying two serving points before changing lesson transitions. This requires a staffing check, and it may not solve the problem. If the late-served pupils still have too little time, the extra minutes should be reconsidered. The survey raised the question; observation helped us choose the first change to test. Neither should be ignored, but they do different jobs.

workedSolution: The survey shows pupils feel hurried, while queue timing indicates where the pressure arises.
Both contribute evidence of different kinds without proving the serving-point solution in advance.
reviewFocus: Independently solve without the key; check each alternative and the stated conditions.
Review originality, vocabulary, difficulty and time for an above-average Year 5/6 learner.
